content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Define exothermic reactions in terms of energy transfer
Identify common types of exothermic reactions
Draw and interpret energy level diagrams for exothermic reactions
Describe practical applications of exothermic reactions
release energy to the surroundings, usually as heat. They are extremely common and include some of the most important reactions in chemistry, from burning fuels to the reactions in our bodies.
Energy released by forming new bonds > Energy required to break old bonds
Net energy is released to the surroundings

The combustion of propane releases 2220 kJ of energy per mole. Write the thermochemical equation.
Draw an energy level diagram for the combustion of methane (ΔH = -890 kJ/mol).

Energy
   ↑
   |  CH₄ + 2O₂ (Reactants)
   |      |
   |      | 890 kJ released
   |      ↓
   |  CO₂ + 2H₂O (Products)
   |
   └──────────────────→ Progress of reaction
Explain why neutralisation reactions are always exothermic.
In neutralisation, H⁺ ions react with OH⁻ ions
They form water: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O
The O-H bonds formed in water are very strong
More energy is released forming these bonds than is needed to break the original bonds
A student adds zinc to copper sulfate solution. The temperature rises from 22°C to 38°C. Calculate the temperature change and explain whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
Temperature increased, so surroundings got hotter
Energy was released from the reaction
Energy is released (transferred) TO the surroundings as heat
Drawing the energy diagram with products above reactants
For exothermic, products are LOWER (less energy)
Writing ΔH as positive for exothermic
ΔH is always NEGATIVE for exothermic reactions

a) Calculate the temperature change. (1 mark)
b) Explain why the temperature changed. (2 marks)

Reaction between an acid and a base

Applications: hand warmers, self-heating cans, heating fuels
